en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on Similes, Section on the Water Jar.
3. The Question on the Six-Limbed Parasol “Venerable Nāgasena, when you say that ‘three qualities of the parasol should be adopted,’ which are those three qualities that should be adopted?
“Just as, Great King, the parasol moves above the head;”
In the same way, Great King, the practitioner of yoga must walk upon the very heads of the defilements.
This, Great King, is the first quality of the parasol that should be adopted.
Furthermore, Great King, the parasol provides support for the head.
In the same way, Great King, a practitioner of yoga must cultivate the support of wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*).
This, Great King, is the second quality of the parasol to be adopted.
Furthermore, Great King, the parasol wards off wind, heat, clouds, and rain.

In the same way, Great King, the yogi, the practitioner of yoga, must ward off the winds of the opinions of various sectarian recluses and brahmins, as well as the rains of the three kinds of fires, heat, and defilements.
This, Great King, is the third quality of the sunshade that should be adopted.
And this, Great King, was said by the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma:
"Just as a large umbrella,
without holes and firmly constructed,
wards off the wind and the heat,"
Just as there are great showers of rain,
so too is the Son of the Buddha pure,
wearing the umbrella of virtue.
"It wards off the rain of defilements;
it is the means for overcoming the threefold fever.
Thus ends the third question on the umbrella.
